headline: Medium prompt-injection and cascading-error risk from Firecrawl’s raw web content flowing into Pipecat’s shared-bus, multi-service voice pipeline.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Firecrawl ingests web content and exposes scrape/search/agent APIs, while Pipecat has text/LLM transports and a shared bus. That creates a plausible default path where attacker-controlled page content reaches Pipecat as instructions. No direct provenance or isolation is documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Firecrawl output is forwarded into Pipecat prompts or tool messages without provenance tags
IF Pipecat parses scraped text as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Add a fixed system prompt that treats Firecrawl output as untrusted data
Strip HTML/markdown instructions before passing content onward
Insert a provenance marker on all Firecrawl-derived fields
Disable any auto-execute tool path for scraped content
requires-engineering: add content-safety filtering between the agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Firecrawl touches API keys, screenshots, and structured data; Pipecat touches conversation state, audio/video, and analytics, and can run across a shared bus. If they share a workspace or bus, sensitive material can cross boundaries. The profiles do not prove isolation, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents share a filesystem, message bus, or transcript store
IF Firecrawl outputs include API keys, screenshots, or structured data that Pipecat logs or forwards
mitigations: Separate workspaces and log directories
Redact secrets before handoff
Turn off verbose transcript logging
Restrict Pipecat outputs to non-sensitive summaries
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on shared storage

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Firecrawl has broad network egress and supports multiple instances; Pipecat has allowlisted egress and shared-bus concurrency. Their mutable surfaces differ, but overlapping networked workflows can still conflict over shared resources or state. Because locking/isolation is not documented, uncertainty warrants medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same downstream API, queue, or datastore
IF multiple instances of either agent operate on shared mutable state without locks
mitigations: Assign separate resource namespaces
Serialize writes through one coordinator
Use per-agent API credentials
Disable concurrent writes to shared targets
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency or locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Firecrawl can generate scraped facts and Pipecat includes LLM, transport, and action-oriented services. If Pipecat treats Firecrawl output as authoritative, errors or prompt injections can cascade into spoken or downstream actions. The default multi-service pipeline makes this dangerous enough for high severity.
conditions: IF Pipecat uses Firecrawl output as direct context for LLM or transport actions
IF no verification step checks scraped facts before acting or speaking
mitigations: Require a verification step before acting on scraped facts
Mark Firecrawl output as untrusted in prompts
Limit Pipecat to read-only narration of retrieved content
Add human review for high-impact actions
requires-engineering: implement source-citation validation

E_compliance.rationale: Firecrawl touches API keys and web content, while Pipecat handles conversation state and analytics/metrics. The profiles do not document residency, retention, or certification alignment, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because uncertainty escalates and the pair could process regulated data, medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated or personal data is routed through both agents
IF retention, logging, or residency policies differ between Firecrawl and Pipecat deployments
mitigations: Avoid routing regulated data through the pair
Disable analytics logging where possible
Document retention settings for both agents
Confirm residency and DPA coverage before deployment
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across both systems
